# Reading the Project Structure Generated by Initializr

When you create your first Spring Boot project with **Spring Initializr**, you receive a skeleton that can compile and run immediately. This skeleton already handles many initial tasks: setting up the build tool, declaring Spring Boot and your chosen dependencies, creating the application entry point, and preparing locations for configuration and tests. Knowing how to read the project structure helps you understand **what each file is responsible for, which files to edit when developing a feature, and which files are tool-generated**.

This lesson uses an illustrative project named `demo`, **Java** as the language, **Gradle (Groovy DSL)** as the build tool, **JAR** packaging, and `com.example.demo` as the root package. Maven or Gradle Kotlin DSL projects have some different files; the corresponding parts are explained separately. Exact files depend on Initializr selections and the Spring Boot version, so your actual structure may be shorter or longer than the example.

## 1. What does Spring Initializr generate?

[Spring Initializr](https://start.spring.io/) is a project initialization tool. You choose basic metadata and dependencies, then download the project to open in your IDE.

| Field at Project Creation | Example | Typical Impact on the Skeleton |
|---|---|---|
| **Project** | Gradle - Groovy / Gradle - Kotlin / Maven | Determines the build configuration files and build tool wrapper. |
| **Language** | Java | Determines the source language and extensions of primary source files. |
| **Spring Boot** | A Boot version supported by Initializr | Determines framework, plugin, and managed dependency versions. |
| **Group** | `com.example` | Typically used as the artifact's `group`/`groupId` and helps form the default package. |
| **Artifact** | `demo` | Artifact name, default directory/output filename, and usually part of the project name. |
| **Name** | `demo` | Display name of the project; may affect the root project name depending on build tool. |
| **Description** | `Demo project for Spring Boot` | Descriptive metadata for the project. |
| **Package name** | `com.example.demo` | Root package and directory path where generated Java files are placed. |
| **Packaging** | JAR | Defines the artifact format; choosing WAR has different integration points/configuration. |
| **Java** | 17 or 21, depending on Boot version | Sets the Java version target/toolchain in the project configuration. |
| **Dependencies** | Spring Web, Validation, Spring Data JPA... | Adds corresponding libraries/starters to the build declaration; may generate related configuration or documentation hints. |

**Initializr creates the skeleton, not the complete business application.** If you select Spring Web, you get the libraries to build HTTP APIs, but you still have to write the controllers yourself. If you select Spring Data JPA, you get the data-access foundation, but you do not automatically get entities and repositories for your problem.

## 2. Viewing the entire directory tree

The example below illustrates a basic Gradle Java project. Some folders such as `static/`, `templates/`, or files like `.gitignore` may or may not be present depending on the skeleton; they are noted as **optional** where relevant.

```text
demo/
├── gradle/
│   └── wrapper/
│       ├── gradle-wrapper.jar
│       └── gradle-wrapper.properties
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/
│   │   │   └── com/
│   │   │       └── example/
│   │   │           └── demo/
│   │   │               └── DemoApplication.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       ├── application.properties
│   │       ├── static/             # May not exist yet or may be empty
│   │       └── templates/          # May not exist yet or may be empty
│   └── test/
│       └── java/
│           └── com/
│               └── example/
│                   └── demo/
│                       └── DemoApplicationTests.java
├── .gitattributes              # If provided by Initializr
├── .gitignore                  # If provided by Initializr
├── build.gradle
├── gradlew
├── gradlew.bat
├── settings.gradle
└── HELP.md                     # If provided by Initializr
```

If you choose **Gradle Kotlin DSL**, the two configuration files typically change to `build.gradle.kts` and `settings.gradle.kts`. If you choose **Maven**, the main files are `pom.xml`, `mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd`, and `.mvn/wrapper/` instead of the Gradle equivalents; the `src/main` and `src/test` trees retain the same meaning.

Do not treat the tree diagram as a rigid checklist across every Initializr version. Look for the **key landmarks** first: the build file in the root folder, `src/main/java`, `src/main/resources`, `src/test`, and the class containing `main()`.

## 3. The four most important areas

A quick way to read a project is to group files by responsibility:

| Area | Responsibility | When Do You Typically Edit It? |
|---|---|---|
| **Build file in the root folder** (`build.gradle`, `pom.xml`, ...) | Defines plugins, dependencies, Java target, build/test/packaging. | When adding libraries, changing versions, or configuring build tasks. |
| **`src/main/java`** | Java source code of the application. | When writing controllers, services, Java configuration, models, and business logic. |
| **`src/main/resources`** | Resources packaged with the application on the classpath. | When editing configuration, messages, templates, static assets, or runtime resource files. |
| **`src/test`** | Test code and test resources. | When writing unit tests, integration tests, or test-specific configuration. |

The `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, `mvnw`, and `mvnw.cmd` files are **wrappers** that invoke the build tool version configured for the project. They do not replace application code and are not normally where you add dependencies.

## 4. Application entry point: `DemoApplication.java`

Open `src/main/java/com/example/demo/DemoApplication.java`:

```java
package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

Each part has its own meaning:

1. **`package com.example.demo;`** defines the Java namespace. By convention, the `com/example/demo` directory structure mirrors this package.
2. **`@SpringBootApplication`** is the central annotation of a Boot application. In terms of primary effect, it combines configuration declaration, enabling auto-configuration, and component scanning with default scope.
3. **`main(String[] args)`** is the Java entry point; this is the method the Java launcher uses to start the application.
4. **`SpringApplication.run(...)`** bootstraps the Spring application, creates and refreshes the `ApplicationContext`, configures components, and starts the server when the project has an appropriate web stack.

The `main()` method does not directly handle HTTP requests. For a web application, requests go through the server and Spring MVC/WebFlux components determined by dependencies and configuration.

### Why does the main class's package matter?

By default, Spring Boot uses the package containing `@SpringBootApplication` as the root for component scanning. A common suitable layout is:

```text
src/main/java/com/example/demo/
├── DemoApplication.java
├── controller/
│   └── GreetingController.java
├── service/
│   └── GreetingService.java
└── model/
    └── Greeting.java
```

Classes in `com.example.demo.controller`, `com.example.demo.service`, and subpackages typically fall within the scanning scope. If you place `GreetingService` in a completely different package, such as `org.other.service`, Spring may not automatically discover that bean under the default scan scope. In that case, revisit package placement or configure scanning explicitly rather than assuming the service annotation is broken.

The names `controller`, `service`, and `model` are conventions for organizing code, **not directories pre-generated by Initializr or mandatory Spring Boot package names**. Larger applications may choose to organize by feature or domain.

### An example of adding a controller after project creation

If you selected a dependency supporting Spring MVC, you can create `src/main/java/com/example/demo/controller/GreetingController.java`:

```java
package com.example.demo.controller;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class GreetingController {

    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello from Spring Boot";
    }
}
```

When running an application with an HTTP server on the default port, you can test `http://localhost:8080/hello`. If the project did not select an appropriate web dependency, the controller annotations or embedded server may not be available; that is governed by the build file, not merely by naming a folder `controller`.

## 5. `src/main/resources`: resources and configuration

`resources` is the place for non-Java files that need to be on the classpath when the application runs. Resources under `src/main/resources` are normally copied into the build output by Gradle/Maven during the build.

### `application.properties` and `application.yml`

An Initializr Java project typically includes `src/main/resources/application.properties`, initially empty. This is the standard place to configure the application:

```properties
spring.application.name=demo
server.port=8081
logging.level.com.example.demo=DEBUG
```

If using YAML, the file can be `application.yml`:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: demo
server:
  port: 8081
logging:
  level:
    com.example.demo: DEBUG
```

These two snippets illustrate **the same configuration information**, and do not need to coexist in the same project. Choose a clean approach to avoid duplicate configuration where it is hard to tell which value takes effect. Actual configuration can also come from command-line arguments, environment variables, Java system properties, and profile-specific files.

Files like `application-dev.properties` or `application-prod.yml` **are not required out of the box**; you add them when you need environment-specific configuration. Never put real passwords, access tokens, or secrets into configuration files committed to a repository. You can use placeholders supplied from the environment at runtime, such as:

```properties
app.api-key=${APP_API_KEY}
```

The example above is only useful if a component in your application reads `app.api-key` and the `APP_API_KEY` environment variable is properly provided at startup.

### `static/` and `templates/`

These two directories are sometimes pre-created or shown by IDEs as conventional locations:

- **`static/`**: typically holds CSS, JavaScript, images, and static files served directly by the web framework when appropriate configuration/dependencies are present.
- **`templates/`**: typically holds server-side templates, such as Thymeleaf, when the project has a matching template engine.

Simply having a `templates/` directory **does not mean** Spring Boot will automatically render HTML. You need a template engine dependency and a controller returning the corresponding view name. Likewise, having a `static/` directory does not cause a non-web application to create an HTTP server.

### Other resources that may appear later

You may later add `messages.properties` for message bundles, SQL migration files, certificates, logger configurations, or sample data depending on your needs. These folders are not evidence that Initializr is required to generate all of them. Distinguish resources **you add** from **initial skeleton** resources.

## 6. Gradle build file: `build.gradle`

With the Gradle Groovy DSL option, `build.gradle` is the file that declares how the project is built. An illustrative configuration for a Spring Boot project using Spring MVC might look like:

```groovy
plugins {
    id 'java'
    id 'org.springframework.boot' version '3.3.0'
    id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.5'
}

group = 'com.example'
version = '0.0.1-SNAPSHOT'

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web'
    testImplementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test'
}

tasks.named('test') {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
```

This is an **example configuration from a specific Spring Boot generation**, not a claim that current Initializr always produces these exact lines or versions. When working on a real project, keep the compatible versions generated by Initializr. BOM/dependency management and starter names can change across Boot versions.

Configuration blocks to know:

| Block | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `plugins` | Enables Java support and Spring Boot build/run/packaging capabilities. |
| `group`, `version` | Artifact identification metadata. |
| `java.toolchain` | Requests the Java toolchain configured for Gradle; distinct from merely checking `java -version` in the shell. |
| `repositories` | Sources where Gradle looks up dependencies during resolution. |
| `dependencies` | Dependencies declared for runtime, compile, or test per the respective configuration. |
| `tasks.named('test')` | Customizes the test task, for instance to use JUnit Platform. |

Dependencies like `implementation` are typically used for application code; `testImplementation` is for tests. A **Spring Boot starter** bundles commonly paired dependencies so developers do not have to list every individual small library. When you need HTTP JSON, an embedded server, validation, or database access, check which starters are declared rather than guessing from Java filenames.

An example of adding a dependency might look like:

```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-validation'
}
```

You should add the declaration to the build file and run Gradle sync/refresh so the IDE picks up the dependency. Do not manually copy JARs into `src/main/java`.

### `settings.gradle`: build identity and structure

In a single-module Gradle project, the contents are usually simple:

```groovy
rootProject.name = 'demo'
```

In a Gradle multi-project build, this file can also declare subprojects via `include(...)`. **`settings.gradle` is not where you write controllers or configure HTTP settings**. It describes top-level build structure.

### Gradle wrapper: `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, and `gradle/wrapper/`

The wrapper allows running Gradle matching the project's configuration even if Gradle is not installed globally on the machine. It includes OS-specific launch scripts and wrapper files supporting downloading/running the specified Gradle distribution.

```bash
# Linux/macOS
./gradlew tasks
./gradlew test
./gradlew bootRun
./gradlew bootJar
```

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.\gradlew.bat tasks
.\gradlew.bat test
.\gradlew.bat bootRun
.\gradlew.bat bootJar
```

`tasks` lists useful tasks in the build; `test` runs configured tests; `bootRun` runs the application from the project; `bootJar` creates an executable JAR when the Spring Boot plugin and appropriate packaging are used. The wrapper typically downloads the Gradle distribution on first use, so it needs access to the download source and a suitable Java setup.

Wrapper files and build configuration **should usually be version-controlled alongside source code** so others build with the same environment. Output directories like `build/` are normally ignored because they are products generated from source.

## 7. If you chose Maven, what should you read?

With Maven, the main file at the root directory is `pom.xml` (*Project Object Model*). A simplified model:

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
         https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.3.0</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>demo</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

This is also an example to recognize tag roles, not a complete POM for every Boot version. The `parent`, `dependencies`, `build/plugins`, and `properties` elements correspond to metadata, dependencies, plugins, and Java settings. With the Maven wrapper, basic commands are:

```bash
./mvnw test
./mvnw spring-boot:run
./mvnw package
```

Windows PowerShell uses `./mvnw.cmd` or `.\mvnw.cmd` instead of `./mvnw`. Maven artifacts normally appear under `target/`, unlike Gradle's `build/libs/`.

**The commonalities outweigh the differences:** both Maven and Gradle organize runtime code in `src/main/java`, resources in `src/main/resources`, tests in `src/test`, and metadata/dependencies in the build file. You do not need to learn both build tools at once to understand your first Spring Boot skeleton.

## 8. `src/test`: what does the generated test tell you?

Initializr typically generates a test class in the corresponding package, for example:

```java
package com.example.demo;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;

@SpringBootTest
class DemoApplicationTests {

    @Test
    void contextLoads() {
    }
}
```

With an appropriate test engine and test dependency, `@SpringBootTest` requests that the Spring application context be started for the test. The `contextLoads()` method can have an empty body: its initial purpose is to verify that the application context starts up successfully. This is **not a complete test suite for business logic or HTTP APIs**.

When you add controllers, services, or data access, you will need tests with specific assertions to verify expected behavior. You can also place test configuration files under `src/test/resources` as needed; that directory is not necessarily created upfront.

Note: a test that starts the full context can fail when a database, environment variable, or external service is missing. If tests suddenly fail after adding a dependency, inspect both auto-configuration and test configuration; do not assume `contextLoads()` was written incorrectly.

## 9. Output directories that appear after building

Right after extracting an Initializr project, the `build/` or `target/` directory may not exist yet. They are created when running the relevant tasks.

With Gradle:

```text
demo/
└── build/                     # Appears after running a build
    ├── classes/               # Compiled classes
    ├── resources/             # Processed/copied resources
    ├── reports/               # Build/test reports when generated
    ├── test-results/          # Test execution results when generated
    └── libs/                  # JARs if the packaging task was run
```

With Maven, the corresponding directory is typically named `target/`. The JAR file in `build/libs` or `target` is an **artifact built from source and dependencies**, not a place where you directly edit Java code.

A path from source to running application:

```text
src/main/java/*.java ── compile ──> .class
src/main/resources/* ────────────> resources in artifact
dependencies from build file ──────> classpath / packaged libraries
                               │
                               ▼
                     executable JAR (if building a JAR)
                               │
                               ▼
                         java -jar ...
                               │
                               ▼
                    Spring Boot application
```

For a Spring Boot executable JAR, dependency libraries and `.class` files are normally arranged into a packaging layout designed for the Boot loader. This differs from creating a plain Java `.jar` archive; choosing the `jar` or `bootJar` task can produce artifacts with different purposes.

## 10. Reading `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes`, and `HELP.md`

These are files supporting the development workflow, not runtime logic components:

- **`.gitignore`**: tells Git to ignore build outputs, caches, or certain local files. For example, `build/` and `target/` should usually not be committed. Having a `.gitignore` does not mean everything else in the project has already been committed.
- **`.gitattributes`**: defines how Git handles file attributes, such as line endings or text/binary treatment, useful when working across platforms.
- **`HELP.md`**: reference documentation provided by Initializr in some configurations, typically containing links to build tool docs, Spring Boot guides, or the selected dependencies.

Many IDEs create additional `.idea/`, `.project`, `.classpath`, `.settings/`, `.vscode/`, or other metadata after import. Those are usually development environment files, **not part of the original Initializr skeleton**. Whether to commit them depends on team convention; what matters is distinguishing their origin and responsibility.

## 11. A walkthrough for reading and running a newly received project

Suppose you just downloaded the ZIP from Initializr and extracted it into the `demo` folder. Before writing your first controller, follow this order:

**Step 1 — Identify the build tool.** If `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts` is present, the project uses Gradle. If `pom.xml` is present, it uses Maven. Read that file to check the Java target, plugins, and current dependencies.

**Step 2 — Locate the Java entry point.** Open `src/main/java/.../DemoApplication.java`, check the package, `@SpringBootApplication`, and the `SpringApplication.run(...)` call. Note the root package before creating additional controllers/services.

**Step 3 — Inspect configuration.** Open `src/main/resources/application.properties` or `application.yml`. If empty, that does not mean the application lacks configuration: Spring Boot provides many defaults and auto-configurations depending on the classpath.

**Step 4 — Run tests.** With the Gradle wrapper:

```bash
./gradlew test
```

Or with the Maven wrapper:

```bash
./mvnw test
```

If tests fail, read the log messages and test output to find the cause before modifying the project. On Windows, use the corresponding `.bat`/`.cmd` wrapper script.

**Step 5 — Run the application in development mode.** With Gradle:

```bash
./gradlew bootRun
```

With Maven:

```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:run
```

If an appropriate web starter is present, the console typically logs that the embedded server has started and reports the listening port. If no web stack was selected, the application may initialize the context and exit without **any HTTP endpoint**; that is not necessarily an error.

**Step 6 — Build the artifact.** With Gradle:

```bash
./gradlew bootJar
```

With Maven:

```bash
./mvnw package
```

Check `build/libs/` or `target/` to see the actual JAR filename. You can then run **the exact executable JAR that was generated**:

```bash
java -jar path/to/your-application.jar
```

The JAR name can include `artifact`, `version`, and classifiers depending on build configuration. Do not assume every build is named `demo.jar` or every `.jar` file is an executable JAR.

## 12. Where should your first changes go?

| What Do You Want to Do? | Typical Location to Open | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| Add a `GET /hello` endpoint | Create a Java controller under the root package. | Spring MVC reads mapping annotations from registered controllers. |
| Add business processing logic | Create a Java service per project structure. | Separates business logic from HTTP transport. |
| Change the server port | `application.properties`/`application.yml` or environment configuration. | This is a runtime application property. |
| Add a database driver | The build file. | A driver is a dependency that needs to be resolved. |
| Create server-rendered HTML pages | `templates/`, a controller, and an appropriate template engine dependency. | Templates need a rendering engine to produce responses. |
| Add static CSS/JS | `src/main/resources/static/` when supported by the web stack. | Places assets where static web resources can be served. |
| Add tests for controllers/services | `src/test/java`. | Keeps test source separate from runtime code. |
| Change target Java version | Toolchain/Java version settings in the build file. | The build tool compiles according to the target. |
| Rename a Gradle project | Usually `settings.gradle`/`settings.gradle.kts`. | The settings file declares the root project name. |

Do not edit compiled classes in `build/classes` or files in `build/libs` expecting those edits to survive the next build. The basic rule is **edit source code or source configuration, then rebuild the artifact**.

## 13. Common misconceptions when first opening a project

### “Having `DemoApplication.java` means I already have a REST API”

Not necessarily. The main file bootstraps the application. To have an HTTP API, you need an appropriate web dependency, a running server, and a controller/router declaring endpoints. If `/hello` returns 404, check mappings and package scanning before suspecting Initializr is broken.

### “Adding a dependency by importing a class in the IDE”

`import` in Java only states that you want to use a type already accessible on the compile classpath; it does not download new libraries from Maven Central. You must declare the dependency in `build.gradle`/`pom.xml`, let the build tool resolve it, and sync the project in the IDE.

### “The `resources` folder is only for images and HTML”

No. It holds many kinds of resources on the runtime classpath, notably `application.properties`, `application.yml`, message bundles, and framework configuration resources. `static/` and `templates/` are simply two convention-based subfolders for web applications.

### “The application is running because the build command succeeded”

`build` or `package` confirms that the build tasks completed for that run, **not that an application is left running to serve requests**. The `bootRun` task, `java -jar` command, or IDE Run action directly starts the application. Distinguish build-time from runtime.

### “Running via `bootRun` and `java -jar` are always identical”

Both run the Java application, yet they can differ in classpath, argument passing, environment, working directory, and input artifact. When one launch method succeeds and the other fails, compare those factors.

### “Renaming a package just means renaming the directory”

Java packages live in the `package` declaration of each file; renaming requires updating source locations, `package` declarations, imports, and related configuration/references. In Spring Boot, you must also consider component scan scope. Use your IDE's **Refactor/Rename** feature whenever possible.

### “Delete the wrapper because my machine already has Gradle/Maven”

The wrapper ensures teammates and CI systems use the build tool version specified by the project, so it is usually worth keeping in version control. Using a global Gradle/Maven installation can work, but does not guarantee the same version and compatible behavior with the project.

## 14. Self-guided exercises to explore the Initializr skeleton

**Exercise A — Map the files.** Create a Java Gradle JAR project with the Spring Web dependency. Open the extracted folder and write down the actual filenames corresponding to the four areas: build file, main Java, resources, and test Java. Mark which folders from this lesson's example **do not exist** in your generated project; that helps distinguish optional items from required ones.

**Exercise B — Trace dependency impact.** Generate two skeletons with identical metadata: one with Spring Web and one without. Compare **dependency declarations in the build file**, then run both applications and observe the difference regarding the HTTP server. No framework code edits are needed to produce this difference.

**Exercise C — Add a simple endpoint.** Create a `/hello` controller under a subpackage of the class with `@SpringBootApplication`. Run the application, access the endpoint, then change `server.port` in the configuration file and re-check the URL. Connect the three items modified: Java source, configuration file, and running process.

**Exercise D — Inspect the artifact.** Run `bootJar` or `package` and locate the JAR in the respective build tool's output folder. Compare the directory tree **before** and **after** building; identify which files belong to source and which are regenerable outputs.

## 15. Takeaways to start development

A project generated by Initializr is an **executable blueprint**, not merely a collection of folders. The build file specifies *what the project needs to build*; `src/main/java` contains *application logic and the entry point*; `src/main/resources` holds *runtime configuration and resources*; `src/test` holds *behavior checks*; and the wrapper lets *others run builds matching project configuration*.

When encountering an unfamiliar file, identify whether it belongs to **source**, **runtime resources**, **build configuration**, **tests**, or **generated output**. That classification is enough to read a new Initializr skeleton, pick the right place to make changes, and develop Spring Boot without depending on which folders your IDE happens to display.
